title: Cyril, Methodius and Valentine (14 February)
hookLine: the calendar keeps the brothers of the Slavs on the same day as Valentine, a Roman martyr

cards: Shop windows on the fourteenth of February: red hearts, roses in plastic sleeves, cards with a little winged boy and his bow.
Open the Church's calendar to the same square, and the first names printed there are two brothers from the Greek world who gave a people an alphabet: Cyril and Methodius.
Somewhere below them, in the old list of martyrs, is a Roman called Valentine. So the day holds two gifts side by side. Love, and letters.

teach.h: A PEOPLE WITHOUT A WRITTEN LANGUAGE.
teach.b: Tradition says the brothers grew up in Thessalonica, in Greece, and were sent north to the Slavic peoples, who had no written form of their own language.
Preaching to someone in a borrowed language is like singing a song in a key they can't reach.

So the brothers did something patient and strange: they built an alphabet. With it they translated the Gospels and the prayers of the liturgy into the people's own Slavonic speech. Not everyone liked it.

teach.h: ROME LETS THE SLAVONIC BOOKS BE USED.
teach.b: Tradition says some churchmen argued that worship belonged only in the old sacred languages, so the brothers traveled to Rome to make their case, and the pope received them and let the Slavonic books be used.
Cyril, the younger, died in Rome. Methodius went back and kept working. A line in the Acts of the Apostles, from Pentecost, sounds like their whole life.

In the Douay-Rheims, the crowd says: "we have heard them speak in our own tongues the wonderful works of God." The Church remembers them as apostles of the Slavs and keeps them among the patron saints of Europe.

teach.h: VALENTINE: A MARTYR WE KNOW LITTLE OF.
teach.b: And Valentine? Honestly, very little is known.

teach.h: IN OUR OWN TONGUES THE WONDERFUL WORKS OF GOD.
teach.b: He is remembered as a Roman martyr. The hearts, the cards and the birds pairing off came later, from customs and poems, not from anything we know of his life.
Still, the two belong on one day: to give someone words in their own language is a way of loving them.

how: Catholics in the Roman calendar keep 14 February as the memorial of Saints Cyril and Methodius, patrons of Europe, while Valentine is remembered in the Roman Martyrology; Slavic Catholic and Orthodox communities celebrate the brothers with special honor.

games.q: you've been sent to preach to a people whose language has never been written down. what do you do?
o: teach them a language that already has books.
build an alphabet for their own language.
preach out loud only and never write anything.
games.why: the brothers built an alphabet and translated the Gospels and the liturgy into Slavonic, and took their case to Rome when it was challenged.

practice: Bring one person to mind and ask what their language is: some people hear love in words, some in a cooked meal, a fixed bike, or a message that just says thinking of you.
Choose the thing they'd understand, not the thing easiest for you to give. If you pray, hold them before God for a moment; if you don't, just keep their face in mind.

wordCard.voice: Cyril. With his brother Methodius, the apostle of the Slavs, who gave a people letters for their own language so they could hear the Gospel in it.

orig.note: Greek: Cyril, the name tradition says Constantine took as a monk near the end of his life.
